bill_summary: Regulates the use of prospective tenants' criminal history records by residential landlords with five or more rental units. Prohibits landlords from requiring drug tests, substance use treatment records, or initial criminal history disclosures. Permits landlords to inquire into specified violent and sexual crimes before making an offer. Authorizes landlords to review certain recent felony convictions only after extending a conditional rental offer. Requires landlords to consider applicant evidence of record inaccuracies, rehabilitation, or mitigating factors before withdrawing an offer. Shields landlords from liability for leasing to individuals with criminal records or omitting background checks.
responsible_party: Department of Housing and Community Development; Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs in the Department of Housing and Community Development
stakeholders: Landlords managing or owning five or more residential rental units in Maryland; prospective residential tenants
fiscal_impact_summary: No material impact on State or local finances or operations. A civil penalty of up to $500 per violation applies to violators.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DHCD is the primary implementing agency under the bill. Its Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs is required to develop and publish a model notice document on its website, and the Department is mandated to adopt regulations to carry out the subtitle.

The required model notice informs prospective tenants of their right to file a complaint under § 13-401 of the Commercial Law Article, which falls under the purview of the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General.

The bill creates statutory restrictions and a civil penalty of up to $500 for violations within landlord-tenant law, which may result in filings or enforcement actions adjudicated within the state court system.

Synopsis: Providing that the exemption for owner-occupied residential real property in a bankruptcy proceeding includes certain real property held in a revocable trust; and altering the amount of the exemption for owner-occupied residential real property in a bankruptcy proceeding.
Title: Bankruptcy Proceedings - Exemptions From Execution - Residential Real Property

NarrowSubjects.Name: Elderly Persons (65+) -see also- Elder Abuse and Neglect

bill_summary: Expands the Maryland bankruptcy exemption for owner-occupied residential real property to include residential property held in a revocable trust. Sets the maximum bankruptcy exemption amount for eligible residential real property at $125,000 for an individual. Caps the combined exemption at $125,000 if multiple individuals claim the exemption for the same property in the same proceeding. Requires the exemption amounts to adjust annually based on the Consumer Price Index beginning in fiscal year 2028. Repeals provisions that prohibit repeat exemption claims on the same property within eight years. Applies prospectively to bankruptcy proceedings filed on or after June 1, 2026.
responsible_party: Judiciary (Administrative Office of the Courts)
stakeholders: Individual debtors domiciled in Maryland filing for bankruptcy, settlors of revocable trusts, and creditors
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not directly affect State or local finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article regarding statutory debtor exemptions for residential real property in bankruptcy proceedings. While bankruptcy cases are adjudicated in federal courts, state courts interact with judgment execution and exemption laws, and the Administrative Office of the Courts was consulted for operational review.

Synopsis: Requiring the State Board of Elections and each local board of elections to refer to absentee ballots that are delivered to a voter by the Internet as "print-at-home ballots" in all communications with voters and the general public; providing that absentee ballots are considered timely and may be counted under certain circumstances; and establishing requirements regarding absentee ballots that apply if federal law or a federal court establish requirements for the timeliness of absentee ballots that differ from State requirements.
Title: Election Law - Absentee Ballots - State and Federal Requirements

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Laws and Ordinances -see also- Pub Local Laws; Uniform Laws
Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting

bill_summary: Establishes statutory standards governing when an absentee ballot is considered timely and may be counted. Prohibits counting absentee ballots that do not meet these timeliness requirements. Requires election boards to refer to Internet-delivered absentee ballots as "print-at-home ballots" in public communications. Requires votes in nonfederal contests on timely ballots to be counted if federal timeliness requirements differ. Requires the State Board of Elections to adopt conforming regulations and provide voter notices under differing federal rules.
responsible_party: State Board of Elections; local boards of elections
stakeholders: Maryland voters casting absentee ballots and local boards of elections
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures may increase by an indeterminate amount in FY 2026, by at least $317,000 in FY 2027, and by $182,000 in each future general election fiscal year if federal absentee ballot timeliness requirements differ from State law. Local expenditures may increase by an indeterminate amount in FY 2026, by at least $392,000 in FY 2027, and by $182,000 in each future general election fiscal year. Revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: SB 949 directly amends the Election Law Article and mandates that the State Board of Elections (SBE) establish public communication terminology ('print-at-home ballots'), adopt regulations for absentee ballot canvassing under potential federal conflicts, and execute voter outreach and notification campaigns. SBE also incurs significant fiscal and operational impacts for acquiring additional ballot scanners, modifying the statewide voter registration system, and printing voter notices.

Synopsis: Exempting the driver's seat of a school bus from the requirement that a school bus be constructed with certain materials that enable it to meet all the criteria of the school bus seat upholstery fire block test established by the National School Transportation specifications and procedures adopted by the most recent National Congress on School Transportation.
Title: Education - School Bus - Fire Safety Standards
bill_summary: Exempts the driver's seat of a school bus from seat upholstery fire block test requirements. Relieves driver's seats from specifications adopted by the most recent National Congress on School Transportation. Maintains required fire block materials for school bus passenger seating. Directs the Motor Vehicle Administration to adopt regulations promoting school bus fire safety standards. Takes effect July 1, 2026.
responsible_party: Motor Vehicle Administration; Maryland State Department of Education
stakeholders: local school systems, school bus drivers, and school bus manufacturers and contractors
fiscal_impact_summary: Potential minimal decrease in local school system expenditures for school bus procurement beginning in FY 2027. The Motor Vehicle Administration can update safety inspection procedures with existing resources. No effect on state or local revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration is statutorily tasked under § 7-808 of the Education Article with adopting regulations to promote fire safety standards for school buses and will need to update its vehicle safety inspection procedures to reflect the driver's seat upholstery exemption.

The Department of Education is statutorily designated to advise the Motor Vehicle Administration on the adoption of school bus fire safety standards and oversees public education transportation requirements across Maryland's school districts.

The Department of Transportation is the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration, which regulates school bus safety specifications and inspections, and was consulted on the fiscal and operational impact of the bill.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City to issue Class B beer, wine, and liquor licenses for the odd side of the 1000 block of West Baltimore Street and the even side of the 800 block of North Charles Street in the 40th alcoholic beverages district, subject to certain limitations; and prohibiting certain license holders in a certain area of the 40th alcoholic beverages district from selling alcoholic beverages before 10 a.m. or after 10 p.m.

bill_summary: Authorizes the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City to issue certain Class B restaurant licenses in the 40th district. Permits new Class B licenses on West Baltimore Street and North Charles Street, subject to community agreements. Authorizes the Board to waive member-only sales restrictions for a Class C license on Eutaw Place. Alters geographic boundaries establishing restricted 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. sales hours in the district. Takes effect July 1, 2026.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverages license holders and restaurant owners in the 40th alcoholic beverages district of Baltimore City
fiscal_impact_summary: No state effect. Baltimore City finances and operations are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends provisions of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article concerning alcoholic beverages licenses and hours of sale in Baltimore City. While local licensing and enforcement are administered by the Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners, the Comptroller is the state agency responsible for overseeing alcohol regulation and administering alcoholic beverage taxes.

Synopsis: Specifying that the inspector for the Board of License Commissioners for Caroline County is the county codes administrator or an individual the Board appoints as inspector.
Title: Caroline County - Alcoholic Beverages - Inspector

NarrowSubjects.Name: Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc

bill_summary: Specifies that the inspector for the Caroline County Board of License Commissioners is the county codes administrator or an appointed individual. Authorizes the Board to appoint an individual as inspector. Requires the Board to specify the inspector's duties, including administering and enforcing county alcoholic beverages laws. Requires the inspector's salary to be provided in the county budget. Takes effect July 1, 2026.
responsible_party: Caroline County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Caroline County Board of License Commissioners, the Caroline County codes administrator, and appointed alcoholic beverages inspectors in Caroline County
fiscal_impact_summary: No effect on state finances. Does not materially affect Caroline County finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is responsible for regulating the state's alcohol industry. While this bill specifically addresses the local appointment of the alcoholic beverages inspector for the Caroline County Board of License Commissioners, it pertains to the broader enforcement of alcoholic beverage laws in Maryland.

responsible_party: Howard County Government; Sheriff of Howard County; State's Attorney for Howard County
stakeholders: Sheriff of Howard County, State's Attorney for Howard County, and Howard County government
fiscal_impact_summary: Howard County expenditures increase by approximately $48,000 in fiscal 2027, $96,000 in fiscal 2028, and at least $104,000 annually thereafter to cover higher salary costs. State operations, State finances, and county revenues are unaffected.

bill_summary: Modifies prior authorizations of State debt across multiple previous capital budget acts. Alters authorized uses and scopes of work for specified capital grants. Changes designated grantee names and reallocates certain grant funds among projects. Extends termination deadlines to allow grantees additional time to expend or encumber funds. Removes matching fund requirements for select local capital improvement projects.
responsible_party: Board of Public Works; Department of Budget and Management; Department of General Services
stakeholders: Grant recipients of prior State capital debt authorizations, including local governments, cultural institutions, community development organizations, and healthcare facilities
fiscal_impact_summary: No material effect on State finances. Modifies the conditions, purposes, and deadlines under which existing State capital grant funds may be expended, with potential impact only on local governments that receive grants.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Board of Public Works oversees and certifies matching funds for state debt authorizations and approves capital grants, state contracts, and expenditures modified by this omnibus bill.
DGS administers state capital grants and local legislative initiatives on behalf of the State and the Board of Public Works, and was consulted as an information source for this bill.
DBM is responsible for the state's capital budget planning, supervising budget execution, and monitoring state debt authorizations, and provided information for the fiscal note.
The bill explicitly strikes the requirement that a $10,000,000 grant to Park Heights Renaissance be used in consultation with the Department of Housing and Community Development.
